Stank
stăngk
v. (gave off a stench; used of judgment on Egypt, of hoarded manna, and of a nation's ruined name)
Old English stincan, to emit a smell of any kind, narrowed in English to an offensive one. The Hebrew baash means both to stink and to become odious — a reputation and a smell in one word.

Biblical Definition

Three uses, and each is a judgment. The first plague: “And the fish that was in the river died; and the river stank, and the Egyptians could not drink of the water of the river” (Exo 7:21). Then the frogs: “And they gathered them together upon heaps: and the land stank” (Exo 8:14) — the plague was over and the stench was worse than the plague, because Pharaoh had asked for a delay of one day before relief. Then the manna: “Notwithstanding they hearkened not unto Moses; but some of them left of it until the morning, and it bred worms, and stank: and Moses was wroth with them” (Exo 16:20). Bread given daily and hoarded overnight rots; the same bread kept for the sabbath by God's own command did not. The fourth use carries the Hebrew's other sense, of a name made odious: “when the children of Ammon saw that they stank before David” (2Sa 10:6), after they had shamed his ambassadors. In every case the stench is the visible end of something men thought they had managed.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) gives stink as to emit a strong offensive smell, and stank as its past tense; figuratively, to be odious or offensive, as a name in disrepute.

expand to see more

STINK, v.i. pret. stank or stunk. To emit a strong offensive smell.

2. To be in bad repute; to be odious. They stank before David. 2 Sam. x.

STINK, n. A strong offensive smell.

It bred worms, and stank. Ex. xvi.

Key Scripture

Exo 7:21 — "And the fish that was in the river died; and the river stank, and the Egyptians could not drink of the water of the river; and there was blood throughout all the land of Egypt."

Exo 8:14 — "And they gathered them together upon heaps: and the land stank."

Exo 16:20 — "Notwithstanding they hearkened not unto Moses; but some of them left of it until the morning, and it bred worms, and stank: and Moses was wroth with them."

2Sa 10:6 — "And when the children of Ammon saw that they stank before David, the children of Ammon sent and hired the Syrians of Bethrehob, and the Syrians of Zoba, twenty thousand footmen, and of king Maacah a thousand men, and of Ishtob twelve thousand men."

Modern Corruption

Hoarded manna is the plainest picture in Scripture of trying to secure tomorrow out of today's provision, and it is generally read as a quaint story rather than as an economy.

expand to see more

The manna is not a lesson against saving; the same law that forbade keeping it overnight commanded a double portion gathered on the sixth day, and that portion did not rot. Scripture elsewhere praises the ant and the prudent man, and the seven years of plenty in Egypt were stored on God's own instruction. The sin at Exodus 16:20 is precise: they hearkened not unto Moses. God had said the bread would come every morning, and some of them arranged an insurance against His word. What they kept bred worms by dawn. The distinction the passage draws is between saving under God's direction and saving against God's promise, and it cannot be settled by the size of the store — it is settled by whether a man is obeying or hedging. The Lord's prayer keeps the same rhythm: give us this day our daily bread.

The frogs supply the other lesson, and it is about delay. Moses asked Pharaoh when he should entreat for the removal of the plague, and Pharaoh said, To morrow — one more night with the frogs rather than immediate relief, for reasons the text does not explain and does not need to. The frogs died, were gathered upon heaps, and the land stank. Sin left one more day does not stay the same size; it decays where it lies. That is worth saying plainly to a Christian who intends to deal with something and has decided that tomorrow will do. And the last use, the Ammonites who stank before David, shows a nation discovering that an insult it had enjoyed making was a stench it could not now wash off — so it hired thirty-three thousand men to defend what a word of apology would have settled.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew baash (H887), to stink and to become odious; used of the river, the land, the hoarded manna, and a nation's name.

expand to see more

Hebrew baash (H887) — to have a bad smell, and figuratively to be abhorred; the river stank, and Ammon stank before David; Exodus 7:21, 2 Samuel 10:6.

Hebrew man (H4478) — manna, the bread whose name means what is it; given daily and not to be kept; Exodus 16:15.

Hebrew rimmah (H7415) — a maggot, a worm; it bred worms, and stank; Exodus 16:20.

Hebrew machar (H4279) — to morrow; Pharaoh's answer when offered relief from the frogs; Exodus 8:10.

Greek ozo (G3605) — to smell, to give off odour; by this time he stinketh, said of Lazarus four days dead; John 11:39.

Usage

"“The river stank” — the first plague, at the water Egypt worshipped."

"“It bred worms, and stank” — insurance taken out against a promise."

"“They stank before David” — an insult that could not be washed off."
